newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU gets short shrift at G7 gathering.
newsitem.headline: EMU gets short shrift at G7 gathering.

text.p: Europe's plans for a common currency were shunted aside on Saturday as top officials from the Group of Seven industrialised nations concerned themselves with a robust dollar and Japan's worrying financial situation.

Although the ongoing scramble by European governments to join economic and monetary union (EMU) has prompted a steady stream of headlines in recent days, the four-hour Berlin gathering was nearly devoid of any talk about the euro.
"We spent very little time discussing EMU...Almost no discussion at all," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told a news conference.

When there was commentary, it was mostly aimed at stamping out reports of secret deals to keep out certain countries and at calming worries that Europe's lacklustre growth would lead to a delay in EMU's launch date.
"It is just the start of February. Every country has a chance to meet the criteria," said German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, referring to the preconditions of the single currency.
"Only at the start of next year, when the figures are produced, will we be able to say" who will join, he added.
Countries wishing to join a single currency must bring their budget deficits in line with the Maastricht Treaty during 1997, the year they will be judged for fitness.

European financial markets were buffeted earlier in the week when an article in London's Financial Times suggested European Union monetary officials were hatching a plan to delay Italy's entry into monetary union.

The report unleashed a storm of denials and protests out of leading European capitals and incensed Italian officials who now seem more determined than ever to join EMU in 1999, its expected launch date.
Summing up the views of many EU finance ministers, France's Jean Arthuis said any country that did not join right away should enter as soon as possible.
In the recent past, such high-level gatherings have sparked interest from countries outside Europe over the potential effects the EMU might have on their economic well being.

But when asked whether there was any concern from the United States, Japan or Canada about the future impact of the euro, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, said the three members had not even brought the subject up.
"It seems to me the three non-Europeans felt no need to initiate a discussion (on the euro)," Clarke said.

He added that German Finance Minister Theo Waigel gave a report about a meeting of EU leaders in Dublin last December, at which agreement was reached on a budget stability pact and a new Exchange Rate Mechanism.

EU officials, however, say that the external implications of the euro, such as its potential role as a major reserve currency and impact on global trade and portfolio flows, are likely to soon focus the minds of policy-makers.
The very nature of the G7, an informal club of the world's richest nations, will also be altered once a common European currency is formed.

Still unclear, for example, is the position the EU will have in such settings. While many seem to believe the European Commission, as the EU executive might be included, its lack of democratic legitimacy might make this a bit tricky.
